title: Coordination compounds: ligands, geometry and electron counting
subject: Chemistry

sources.title: OpenStax: Lewis acids, bases and formation equilibria

chapters.title: Read brackets, charges and donor atoms
points: Oxidation state + ligand charges = complex charge.
Each neutral bidentate en supplies two donor atoms.
Outer-sphere chloride is not included in the coordination number.
chapters.script: Welcome to Coordination Compounds. This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice. Our first habit is to read the brackets before counting anything. A coordination entity contains a central atom or ion and its directly bonded ligands. A ligand donates an electron pair through a donor atom. Species outside the brackets are counterions, not automatically ligands. Consider the cobalt complex on the board. Three chloride counterions require the bracketed entity to have charge positive three. The abbreviation e n stands for ethane one two diamine. Each of these ligands is neutral, so cobalt has oxidation state plus three. Now count donor atoms separately. Each e n attaches through two nitrogen atoms. Three such bidentate ligands give six directly attached donors. The coordination number is six, not three. Oxidation state, complex charge, ligand count and donor count are four different quantities. Werner's primary valency is associated with oxidation state, while secondary valency is associated with coordination number and directed bonding. Water and ammonia are normally monodentate. A chelating ligand attaches through several donor atoms and forms a ring with the metal. E D T A can bind through six donor atoms in a common hexadentate arrangement. An ambidentate ligand is different: it can use alternative donor atoms. Nitrite can bind through nitrogen or oxygen, but that does not mean it normally binds through both simultaneously. For a second charge check, take hexacyanidoferrate with overall charge negative four. Six cyanide ligands contribute negative six. The iron oxidation state must be plus two to give negative four overall. Write that short charge equation before assigning any electronic configuration. The ligand's charge belongs in the charge balance; its denticity belongs in the donor count.

chapters.title: Name a complex and count ionizable chloride
points: Assume only outer chloride precipitates and the coordination sphere stays intact.
[Co(NH3)4Cl2]Cl: tetraamminedichloridocobalt(III) chloride.
Alphabetize ligand names while ignoring multiplicative prefixes.
chapters.script: Naming becomes easier after charge balance. Name ligands alphabetically, ignoring multiplicative prefixes, then name the metal with its oxidation state in Roman numerals. Ammonia is called ammine, with two m letters, and water is aqua. An anionic complex uses a metal name ending in ate; iron uses ferrate. Thus the potassium salt of the negative four hexacyanidoferrate ion is potassium hexacyanidoferrate, two. The Roman numeral refers to iron's oxidation state, not the ion's charge. Now consider the cobalt salt with four ammonia ligands, two chlorido ligands inside the brackets and one chloride outside. The complex has charge positive one. Four neutral ammonia ligands contribute zero and the two bound chlorides contribute negative two. Cobalt is therefore plus three. Ammine precedes chlorido alphabetically. The name is tetraammine dichlorido cobalt, three, chloride, as written together on the board. Its octahedral geometry allows cis and trans forms; the formula alone does not tell us which one we have. Next, distinguish bound chloride from ionizable chloride. Our worked salt has five ammonia ligands and one chloride inside the brackets, with two chlorides outside. We assume an immediate silver nitrate test that leaves the coordination sphere intact. Under that assumption only the two outer chlorides form silver chloride. A sample containing zero point zero one zero zero mole of salt therefore gives zero point zero two zero zero mole of silver chloride. Multiply by one hundred forty three point five grams per mole to obtain two point eight seven grams. Cobalt is still plus three and its coordination number is six. Counting all three chlorines as precipitated chloride would ignore the test's stated assumption. Bound ligands are not permanently impossible to displace; reaction conditions and time matter. In this question, the intact sphere assumption tells us exactly what to count.

chapters.title: Distinguish geometry and isomerism
chapters.formula: cis: adjacent · trans: opposite · fac-MA3B3: all A–A pairs cis
points: Four donors can give tetrahedral or square-planar geometry.
Linkage changes the donor atom; ionization exchanges bound ion and counterion.
Octahedral fac has mutually cis A donors; mer has one trans A–A pair.
chapters.script: Coordination number is useful, but it does not uniquely fix geometry. Six donors commonly give an octahedral environment. Four can give tetrahedral or square planar geometry. In elementary valence bond language these are described using orbital combinations such as s p three for tetrahedral and d s p two for square planar. These labels are a model, not a complete explanation of spectra. Isomerism needs a separate check. Structural isomers differ in connectivity or in which species lie inside the coordination sphere. Linkage isomers use different donor atoms of an ambidentate ligand. Ionization isomers exchange a coordinated ion with a counterion. A drawing merely rotated on the page is not a new isomer. For square planar platinum with two ammonia and two chloride ligands, adjacent chlorides define the cis form, while opposite chlorides define trans. The angle between the two platinum to chloride bond directions is ninety degrees in cis and one hundred eighty in trans. These are spatial arrangements with the same connectivity. An octahedral complex with three monodentate A ligands and three monodentate B ligands can have facial and meridional forms. In the facial form, the three A donors occupy a triangular face. Every A to metal to A angle is ninety degrees. In the meridional form, one pair of A ligands is opposite, giving a one hundred eighty degree angle. Draw or label the six positions before counting arrangements. Optical isomers are non superimposable mirror images. The cobalt complex with three bidentate e n ligands can form such a pair. Equal amounts of both mirror forms make a racemic mixture with no net optical rotation. That does not make the individual structures identical. Detailed three dimensional optical drawings remain further practice. First establish connectivity and geometry, then ask which particular kind of isomerism is possible.

chapters.title: Fill split orbitals and account for pairing
points: Octahedral t2g electrons contribute −0.4Δo each; eg electrons +0.6Δo each.
High-spin d6: t2g4 eg2, 4 unpaired. Low-spin d6: t2g6, 0 unpaired.
For Δo=250 and P=180 kJ/mol, ELS−EHS=−140 kJ/mol.
chapters.script: Crystal field theory separates the five d orbitals into groups with different energies. In an octahedral field, the three t two g orbitals are lower and the two e g orbitals are higher. Relative to the barycentre, a t two g electron contributes minus zero point four delta octahedral, and an e g electron contributes plus zero point six delta octahedral. Those contributions alone exclude pairing energy. Consider a d six metal ion. If splitting is small compared with the cost of pairing, the high spin arrangement has four electrons in t two g and two in e g. Its orbital occupancy contains four unpaired electrons and one pair. If splitting is sufficiently large, the low spin arrangement puts all six electrons into the lower set as three pairs. There are then no unpaired electrons. Let's calculate the high spin field contribution. Four times minus zero point four, plus two times zero point six, gives minus zero point four delta octahedral. The low spin field contribution is six times minus zero point four, or minus two point four delta octahedral. Now include P as the cost per electron pair. High spin has energy minus zero point four delta plus P. Low spin has minus two point four delta plus three P. Comparing only the negative field terms would miss the extra pairing cost. With delta equal to two hundred fifty kilojoules per mole and P equal to one hundred eighty, high spin gives positive eighty and low spin negative sixty kilojoules per mole on the same chosen energy reference. Low spin minus high spin is negative one hundred forty. Low spin is lower by one hundred forty kilojoules per mole in this simplified model. The crossover is when the octahedral splitting equals the pairing energy. Do not transfer this octahedral orbital diagram unchanged to a square planar or tetrahedral complex.

chapters.title: Connect magnetism, colour and useful chemistry
chapters.formula: μspin-only = √[n(n+2)] μB; n=4 → 4.90 μB; n=2 → 2.83 μB
points: Ni(II) is d8 in both complexes; geometry and electron arrangement differ.
[NiCl4]2−: tetrahedral, 2 unpaired. [Ni(CN)4]2−: square planar, all paired.
Colour may involve d–d or charge-transfer transitions; d count alone is insufficient.
chapters.script: Unpaired electrons produce paramagnetism. An all paired arrangement is diamagnetic. The spin only magnetic moment is the square root of n times n plus two, in Bohr magnetons, where n is the number of unpaired electrons. This is an approximation; orbital contributions can matter. Our high spin octahedral d six example has four unpaired electrons. The square root of four times six is about four point nine zero Bohr magnetons. Low spin d six has no unpaired electrons. Now compare the two nickel complexes on the board. Each has four singly negative ligands and total charge negative two, so both contain nickel in oxidation state plus two. Nickel two has a d eight configuration, after removal of the two four s electrons from neutral nickel. The chloride complex is usually tetrahedral with two unpaired electrons. Its spin only moment is the square root of eight, about two point eight three Bohr magnetons. The cyanide complex is square planar and all paired, so it is diamagnetic. The same metal, oxidation state and coordination number did not guarantee the same geometry or magnetism. Colour needs another check. Absorption between split d levels can remove visible wavelengths, leaving a complementary transmitted or reflected colour. Ligands, oxidation state and geometry affect the splitting. Charge transfer transitions can also produce colour, so d zero or d ten does not guarantee that every compound is colourless. Complex formation is useful in qualitative analysis, including the deep blue copper ammine species in aqueous ammonia, and in biological metal binding, such as iron in haem proteins and magnesium in chlorophyll. Finish with the sequence: complex charge, oxidation state, donor count, d electron count, geometry, then properties. Use the twelve original practice questions and the seven worked examples in the written companion. This is a recorded Unit twelve foundation, not exhaustive coverage or official past paper material.

chapters.title: Ionization and linkage isomerism
chapters.formula: Ionization: exchange sphere / counterion; linkage: change donor atom
chapters.script: Isomerism can change which ion is outside the coordination sphere or which atom binds to the metal. Compare a cobalt complex with five neutral ammonia ligands and coordinated bromide, accompanied by a sulfate counterion, with one containing coordinated sulfate and an external bromide. Cobalt is plus three in each. In the first case, the complex charge is plus two; in the second, it is plus one. The overall elemental inventory is unchanged, but the counterions differ. This illustrates ionization isomerism, assuming the stated coordination spheres persist under the test conditions. Linkage isomerism is different. An ambidentate nitrite ligand can attach through nitrogen or through oxygen, giving different metal to donor connectivity without exchanging the external counterion. Ambidentate does not mean both donor atoms necessarily bind simultaneously to this metal. A bidentate ligand instead supplies two donor attachments in the specified complex. Classify the structural change before applying an isomer name. Formula brackets identify the coordination sphere, so moving a group across a bracket changes chemical information rather than merely changing typography.
points: Ionization · Sphere and counterion · Different free counterion
Linkage · Metal donor attachment · Nitrite: N versus O
Bidentate binding · Two donor attachments · Not just ambidentate

chapters.title: Octahedral fac and mer arrangements
chapters.formula: fac-MA₃B₃: all A pairs cis; mer-MA₃B₃: one A pair trans
chapters.script: For an octahedral complex with three identical A ligands and three identical B ligands, facial and meridional arrangements are distinct geometrical isomers. Imagine six ligand positions on the positive and negative x, y and z axes. Opposite ends of the same axis are trans, while positions on different axes are cis. A facial arrangement places the three A ligands at positive x, positive y and positive z. Every A pair is cis, and the three positions form one face of the octahedron. A meridional arrangement can place A at positive x, negative x and positive z. The first two form a trans pair, while the other two A pairs are cis. The schematic shows these position labels so the classification does not depend on an ambiguous flat sketch. Rotating an entire complex does not create a new isomer. Exchanging ligand positions can. These fac and mer labels apply to this octahedral three plus three pattern; do not reuse them for every six coordinate formula without checking its ligand arrangement.
points: fac · +x, +y, +z · Three cis pairs
mer · +x, −x, +z · One trans; two cis
Opposite pairs · +x/−x; +y/−y; +z/−z · Same axis = trans

chapters.title: Chelation and optical isomerism
chapters.formula: [Co(en)₃]³⁺: three bidentate ligands, six donor attachments
chapters.script: A chelating ligand binds through multiple donor atoms to the same central metal and closes a ring. Ethane one two diamine, commonly abbreviated e n, can bind through its two nitrogen atoms. Three such ligands around cobalt give six donor attachments, so the coordination number is six although there are only three ligand molecules. With neutral diamine ligands and complex charge plus three, cobalt has oxidation state plus three. An octahedral tris chelate arrangement can have two nonsuperimposable mirror image forms, conventionally described by delta and lambda helicity labels. They have the same connectivity but a different three dimensional handed arrangement. Mirror images that can be superimposed do not constitute an optical isomer pair. A flat donor count table alone cannot establish handedness; a spatial model is needed for that assignment. Individual enantiomers can rotate plane polarized light, while an equal mixture has cancelling rotations under the same conditions. Delta and lambda specify structural helicity; they do not automatically predict the sign of measured optical rotation. Keep ligand count, donor count, oxidation state and chirality as separate questions.
points: Ligand molecules · 3 · Each en is bidentate
Coordination number · 6 · Six donor attachments
Optical pair · Δ and Λ · Helicity ≠ rotation sign

chapters.title: Stepwise and overall formation constants
chapters.script: Complex stability is an equilibrium question that needs a defined reaction. Suppose a metal M binds one ligand L to make M L, then binds another to make M L two. Define the first and second stepwise formation constants from those two equilibria. Adding the reactions gives metal plus two ligands forming the bis ligand complex. Multiplying the stepwise constants gives the overall formation constant beta two. With illustrative dimensionless constants ten to the four and ten to the three, beta two is ten to the seven. It is not their sum, and the second constant need not always exceed the first. Thermodynamic constants use activities; concentration ratios are approximations under specified solution conditions. A large overall formation constant favours the complex relative to free metal and free ligand for that defined equilibrium, but the actual composition also depends on ligand availability, competing reactions and mass balances. Thermodynamic stability is distinct from kinetic inertness. A complex can be strongly favoured at equilibrium while exchanging ligands rapidly, or react slowly even when a different product is favoured.
points: M + L ⇌ ML · K₁ = 10⁴ · First binding
ML + L ⇌ ML₂ · K₂ = 10³ · Second binding
M + 2L ⇌ ML₂ · β₂ = 10⁷ · Multiply K₁ and K₂

chapters.title: Coordination in analysis and biology
chapters.formula: Complexation changes speciation; identify metal and ligand roles
chapters.script: Coordination compounds connect reaction chemistry with biological and analytical functions. Chlorophyll contains magnesium in its coordinated pigment framework, while haem groups contain iron in a porphyrin environment. Vitamin B twelve contains cobalt. These metal identities are useful starting facts, but they do not imply that every metal ion has the same biological function in every ligand environment. In qualitative analysis, complex formation can change the concentration of a free metal ion and thereby affect precipitation or dissolution equilibria. Such reasoning requires the competing equilibrium constants and solution conditions. In a standard silver complex example, two cyanide ligands each have charge minus one. A complex charge of minus one therefore places silver at oxidation state plus one. Its formation does not itself require a change in the silver oxidation state. Complex formation is also used in extraction and purification chemistry because ligands can stabilize selected dissolved metal species. Keep ligand binding, redox conversion and precipitation conceptually separate, then connect them through balanced equations when a problem supplies enough data. The purpose here is interpreting chemical roles and charge balance, rather than prescribing an experimental procedure.
points: Chlorophyll · Mg · Biological ligand framework
Haem; vitamin B₁₂ · Fe; Co · Different metal environments

quiz.question: Three bidentate en ligands attached through both donors give coordination number:
quiz.explanation: Each en contributes two donor atoms, giving three times two directly bonded donors.

quiz.question: Iron oxidation state in [Fe(CN)6]^4- is:
quiz.explanation: Six cyanide ligands contribute -6; iron must contribute +2 to give net -4.

quiz.question: In square-planar cis-MA2B2, identical ligands of either type are:
quiz.explanation: Cis places the two like ligands adjacent; trans places them across from each other.

quiz.question: The lower d-orbital set in an octahedral crystal field is:
quiz.explanation: Octahedral splitting places the three t2g orbitals below the two eg orbitals.

quiz.question: An octahedral low-spin d6 arrangement has how many unpaired electrons?
quiz.explanation: All six electrons pair in the three lower t2g orbitals, leaving no unpaired electrons.

quiz.question: Multiplying ligand count by charge gives coordination number:
quiz.explanation: Coordination number counts donor atoms; ligand charge is used in a different charge-balance calculation.

quiz.question: Under an immediate precipitation test that leaves the coordination sphere intact, one mole of [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2 gives how many moles of AgCl?
quiz.explanation: Only the two outer-sphere chloride ions are counted under the stated test conditions; the coordinated chloride remains bound.

quiz.question: The cobalt oxidation state in [Co(NH3)4Cl2]Cl is:
quiz.explanation: The complex cation is +1 and its two chlorido ligands contribute -2, so cobalt contributes +3.

quiz.question: Which ligand is named first in tetraamminedichloridocobalt(III) chloride?
quiz.explanation: Ligands are alphabetized by their names while ignoring multiplicative prefixes; ammine precedes chlorido.

quiz.question: The usual geometry and unpaired-electron count of [NiCl4]^2- are:
quiz.explanation: The tetrahedral nickel(II) d8 chloride complex has two unpaired electrons; coordination number four alone does not imply square planar.

quiz.question: For octahedral d6, including P per electron pair, E_LS - E_HS equals:
quiz.explanation: Low spin gains 2 Delta_o in field energy but introduces two additional electron pairs, costing 2P.

quiz.question: For an octahedral MA3B3 complex with monodentate A and B, a facial arrangement has:
options: All A ligands outside the sphere
quiz.explanation: In the facial form the three A donors occupy one triangular face and are mutually cis. A meridional form contains a trans A-A pair.

quiz.question: A nitrite ligand binding through N in one complex and O in another illustrates:
quiz.explanation: The same ambidentate ligand changes its donor attachment atom.

quiz.question: In octahedral fac-MA3B3, the three A ligands have:
quiz.explanation: The three A positions occupy a face; every A–A pair is cis.

quiz.question: A mer-MA3B3 arrangement with A at +x, −x and +z contains how many A–A trans pairs?
quiz.explanation: The +x and −x positions are opposite; the other A pairs are cis.

quiz.question: For [Co(en)3]3+ with neutral bidentate en, coordination number and oxidation state are:
quiz.explanation: Three bidentate ligands supply six donors; neutral ligands leave cobalt at +3.

quiz.question: Stepwise dimensionless constants K1 = 10^4 and K2 = 10^3 give overall beta2:
quiz.explanation: Adding equilibrium reactions multiplies their constants: beta2 = K1 K2.

quiz.question: Which metal assignment is correct?
options: Chlorophyll: Mg; haem: Fe; vitamin B12: Co
All three contain the same metal
quiz.explanation: The coordinated metal identities are magnesium, iron and cobalt, respectively.
